findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider returns default JCE provider, not BouncyCastle
findings.body: The implementation returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which is the JDK provider that happens to supply the default keystore type (typically SUN/SunJCE), not BouncyCastle. Every other CryptoProvider implementation returns a BouncyCastle/FIPS provider here (DefaultCryptoProvider returns bcProvider, FIPS1402Provider returns bcFipsProvider), and the interface Javadoc on CryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider() explicitly states 'BouncyCastle security provider'. Callers that rely on this getter to obtain a BC-backed Provider will silently receive the JDK provider instead, which can cause missing algorithms, wrong defaults (e.g., signature/padding), or NPEs in downstream code that assumed non-null BC.

findings.title: Dead code allocates and discards two ASN1Encoders in concatenatedRSToASN1DER
findings.body: Lines 114-115 ('ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger); ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);') create two encoders, allocate ByteArrayOutputStream buffers, write the BigIntegers, and immediately discard the results. They are not stored and not part of the DER sequence produced below. They are pure waste (two extra BigInteger.toByteArray() calls and allocations on every ECDSA sign/verify) and clearly look like a leftover from refactoring. They should be removed.

findings.title: order() added as non-default method breaks third-party CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body: CryptoProvider is a public interface in org.keycloak.common.crypto that is implemented by external modules (default/elytron/fips1402) and is part of the published keycloak-common artifact. Adding 'int order();' as an abstract method (instead of a default method) is an ABI break: every third-party or downstream implementation of CryptoProvider will fail to compile against the new release. Since the only purpose of order() is to pick between multiple implementations on the classpath, it should be 'default int order() { return 0; }' (or similar) so existing implementations keep working and the new AuthzClientCryptoProvider can opt in to a lower priority.

findings.title: logger.debugf used with a preformatted message and no parameters
findings.body: The new debug branch builds a StringBuilder of ignored provider names and then calls 'logger.debugf(builder.toString())'. debugf is the parameterized-format API; passing a plain string with no parameters means the string is treated as a format and any stray '%' would throw. It should be 'logger.debug(builder.toString())' (or 'logger.debugf("Ignored crypto providers: %s", joined)'). Same anti-pattern is present on line 63 which is pre-existing but worth aligning.

findings.title: ECDSA conversion test only round-trips, does not validate against known vectors or wrong-key cases
findings.body: ECDSAAlgorithmTest always generates a default-curve (P-256) EC key and runs the same round-trip (DER -> RS -> DER -> RS, equality) for ES256/ES384/ES512. This will pass even if the converter silently produces wrong-length outputs, drops leading bytes incorrectly for edge cases (r or s near q/2, r with high bit set, leading 0x00 from DER INTEGER), or works only because the specific test key avoids boundary values. There is also no test asserting the size of the produced concatenated/DER output, no negative-case test (truncated, malformed), and no test that exercises getBouncyCastleProvider/getKeyStore (whose implementation is actually wrong, see separate finding). Tests against a known signature vector per curve would catch real conversion bugs.
